etymology: From the Fifth Amendment, which says no person shall be compelled to witness against himself - a right, and now a move.
trigger: A question whose answer would be evidence, asked in a room where nobody is being prosecuted.
tell: The answer arrives as a procedure: on the advice of counsel, I decline to answer. It is the same sentence for every question, including the ones that would have cleared him, and it is never followed by a second sentence.
counter: Take the questions the privilege cannot reach - the documents, the staff, the same question to the next witness - and read the refusal into the record by name. The Fifth protects the answer, not the fact that he would not give one.

confused_with.tell: The unawares claims he never knew; the Fifth says he knows and will not say. One leaves a hole in the record, the other puts a wall where the record should be.

senses: The move of answering with a right: the question is put, and what comes back is the Fifth Amendment, in the voice of counsel, identically, for every question on the list.

It works because the privilege is real, and it is his, and it turns a refusal into a status - the silence is lawful, so it cannot be held against him, and it cannot be read either. The right is old and this guide is not against it; the move is what the right becomes when it is the only sentence in the answer, offered in a hearing where what is at stake is a headline, not a cell.
example: *"Forty questions and forty times he **pleaded the Fifth** - including the one about a meeting that was already in his own calendar."*
